fit: concentrated tea extract and olfactory histopathology
assessment: The fourteen-week mouse experiment found more olfactory epithelial and nerve atrophy after concentrated gavage. No odor performance or effect of ordinary brewed tea in Parkinson disease was measured.

fit: separate two-year extract experiment and olfactory histopathology
assessment: Male mouse nerve atrophy and epithelial fibrosis increased across tested extract doses. This refers to the separate two-year cohort and does not count the program's linked short-term report twice. No smell function result.

fit: standardized extract alone or in a mixture in cultured dopaminergic cells
assessment: The cell experiment measured survival and oxidative or inflammatory markers. It uses an extract in culture and mentions human hyposmia only as clinical background.

fit: oral sage tea and global sleep quality in young adults
assessment: The registered study's report gives lower follow-up PSQI with sage than its brown-sugar control. It allocates rooms, gives inconsistent sage baseline values and has protocol differences without the registered threshold responder count. Exact drying method and transfer to Parkinson insomnia are unresolved.

fit: encapsulated dried leaf in Parkinson cognitive impairment
assessment: Five original results pages report the sage-versus-vitamin-E comparison on cognition and salivation, without a sleep or insomnia estimate or a complete adverse-event table.

fit: fresh sage-tip extract and menopause sleep questionnaire outcomes
assessment: Some secondary sleep ratings favored extract. The single menopausal sleep-problems item showed a trend. The extract, population and sleep outcomes differ from dried sage and clinical Parkinson insomnia.

fit: oral unspecified olive oil versus mineral and flaxseed oils in hemodialysis
assessment: Rome III changed 10.3 to 3.2 in the olive-oil group and 10.5 to 4.1 with mineral oil. Group by time p = .15 across arms. The active-comparator result gives no equivalence claim or Parkinson-specific grade contrast.

fit: different olive-oil grades and fecal microbiota in mice
assessment: The author abstract compares extra-virgin and refined olive oil, butter and standard diets using fecal culture and molecular profiling. It supplies no constipation severity or Parkinson outcome.

fit: constipation during a ketogenic program rich in extra-virgin olive oil
assessment: The uncontrolled pediatric epilepsy program reported constipation in 102/389 participants. Many diet components changed and the report has no comparable oil-free or separately assigned oil group.

fit: topical extra-virgin olive oil massage and constipation score
assessment: A randomized nursing-home trial compared oil massage, water massage and usual care. Scores fell most in the oil-massage group. Its administration was topical and no Parkinson-specific result was reported.
